catalog_quote: Young 2024: "Yami has previously been described ([4], [5]) as exhibiting a default pattern of final-syllable stress for most content words. An exception is found in a smaller lexical class of stative verbs (adjectives), most of which take the prefix ma-, which are reported to show stress on the penultimate syllable instead. Simultaneously, however, stress in Yami is described as contrastive and phonemic, and therefore is claimed to be the sole distinguishing feature between minimal pairs such as matá 'eye' and máta 'raw, uncooked,' although such minimal pairs are rare." new_statements.quote: 重音雖然大部分落在最後一個音節，但具有辨義功能。為方便讀者學習，凡出現在其他音節者，在音標層次以重音符號（例如：í，á，é，ó）標示。靜態ma-動詞的詞重音多半落在倒數第二音節，例如：masáray「很高興」、masasáray「每個都很高興」、mapasózi「很令人生氣」、ma'óya「很生氣」、mám'ing「微笑」、mam'im'íngen「很愛笑」、malavlavíin「很愛哭」。加上表程度的詞綴tey-「非常、最」，重音也都落在其後的倒數第二音節，例如：teyméhteng「非常溫暖」、teyráhet「非常壞」、teymálma「最懶惰」。但在正式書寫時，為求精簡，重音則不標記。
new_statements.translation: Although stress mostly falls on the last syllable, it has a meaning-distinguishing (contrastive) function. For the learner's convenience, wherever it falls on another syllable it is marked at the phonetic level with a stress mark (e.g. í, á, é, ó). Word stress in stative ma- verbs mostly falls on the penultimate syllable, e.g. masáray 'very happy', masasáray 'each one is very happy', mapasózi 'very upsetting', ma'óya 'very angry', mám'ing 'smile', mam'im'íngen 'loves to laugh', malavlavíin 'loves to cry'. When the degree affix tey- 'very, most' is added, stress likewise falls on the penultimate syllable after it, e.g. teyméhteng 'very warm', teyráhet 'very bad', teymálma 'laziest'. In formal writing, however, stress is not marked, for concision.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Yami (catalog-all-2026-09-12) has an empty rule field and there are no existing statements; this work supplies the placement (default final, contrastive, with penultimate stress in stative ma- verbs and after tey-). Nothing to contradict.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default word stress is on the final (ultimate) syllable; stress is nonetheless phonemic/contrastive, and the non-final cases are lexically or morphologically specified: stative ma- verbs mostly take penultimate stress, and the degree prefix tey- 'very, most' puts stress on the penult following it. Affixation shifts stress rightward onto a vowel-initial suffix (p.19: pasakay [pa.sa.kaj] + -en -> [pa.sa.ka.jin], 'stress shifts onto the suffix'). The phonological rules on p.22 presuppose final stress: peripheral vowels reduce to schwa in the penult '(non-stressed position)' and schwa deletes in the antepenult '(non-stressed position)'; bound roots and clitics 'obtain stress by attaching to another syllable' (pp.32-33).
new_statements.exceptions: Stative ma- verbs (mostly penultimate stress); degree prefix tey- 'very/most' (stress on the following penult); stress shifts to a vowel-initial suffix under affixation (pasakay -> pasakayin); non-final stress is marked with an acute in the phonetic transcription only, never in formal orthography.
new_statements.identity_note: Rau & Dong 2018 is a pedagogical reference grammar of Yami/Tao (達悟語) as a whole, not tied to one village. Rau & Chang 2006 (ICAL) concerns diphthong variation across Orchid Island villages (Imowrod, Izazaley, Izanomilek and others) and says nothing about stress; no dialect-specific stress claim was found in any work.
